quarterly_data.signal: 80% OF THE WORLD'S DATA NOW SITS ON A HARD DRIVE IN THE DATA CENTER - THE MARKET-STRUCTURE NUMBER SEAGATE'S CALLS DO NOT GIVE. Chairman Dave Mosley on how the business moved from the PC era to mass capacity: 'Now all the data, the mass capacity data we call it, is up in data centers. The boxes that have really morphed, the whole supply chain has had to morph over the last 10 years to the point where 80% of the world's data is on a hard drive in the data center right now, and it's continuing to grow at leaps and bounds.' He attributed the acceleration to AI application breadth rather than any single workload: 'the different applications have just exploded... there's so many different fronts where you've got applications pulling data, creating data, sending it back down'. Seagate's earnings calls quantify its own exabytes and the data-center share of its revenue; this is the installed-base share of world data.
quarterly_data.figure: 80% of the world's data is on a hard drive in the data center right now

quarterly_data.signal: RETENTION ECONOMICS QUANTIFIED FROM SEAGATE'S OWN CIO RESEARCH: 55% SAY DELETING DATA COST THEM MONEY. Chairman Dave Mosley on a study Seagate ran with CIO-level respondents: 'I'll say 55% of the people answering the survey said, I've lost a lot of money because I deleted something that I shouldn't have deleted.' He was explicit that this is not a compliance cost: 'That's not a penalty, that's not because of compliance issues. That's because of opportunity lost, because they deleted something.' Seagate applies the same logic internally - 'Running factories ourselves, we see this every day. If we could only store information about what's going on in the factories for a little bit longer, we believe you can get utility out of that' - and expects the same on customer-acquisition and customer-service data elsewhere. This is the demand-side mechanism (delete-less behaviour) behind the retention narrative the calls assert but never size.
quarterly_data.figure: 55% of the people answering the survey said they lost money by deleting something they should not have deleted

quarterly_data.signal: COLD/OFFLINE STORAGE LOSES ITS ROLE AND NEARLINE BECOMES THE PREFERENTIAL TIER. Asked whether cold storage becomes a non-discussion because data now has to be hot or at least readily accessible, Chairman Dave Mosley drew the line at accessibility rather than temperature: 'We call our products nearline products. These monikers, I don't think we've all come up with the right language yet. But, to me, cold storage means it's so far offline that it's virtually unusable unless a human brings it back... That probably is not going to be very efficient in the future. I think if we can continue to really drive our technology hard and grow exabytes in our industry, then that nearline will become the preferential storage mechanism.' The condition he attaches is Seagate's own areal-density execution - the tier shift only happens if the industry keeps growing exabytes at cost.

OBJECT STORES PLUS METADATA-IN-MEMORY ARE THE ARCHITECTURE CHANGE THAT PUTS UNSTRUCTURED DATA BACK ON HDD TIERS. Chairman Dave Mosley on the stack above the drive: 'down inside the storage layer, we've always been kind of subservient to the file systems and things above us. Now we're starting to see more what I'll call object stores. Where what's really happening at layers above us, in memory layers, say, is that you are having very fast transactions on metadata, then when you need that specific data underneath, you pull it up. That architecture was never really honed before, but it is now. What that means is all of this, the data can be stored cheaper, relatively cheaper, and you can store a lot more of it on the hard drive tiers.' In some cases 'the unstructured data is not even used, it is just the metadata around the unstructured data. You only know which data you need when the algorithm tells you you need it, you pull it up.' He also described the software stack becoming less lossy with fewer handoffs - 'People don't want to pay for that. They want to pay for actually data in the application' - producing 'a stronger tie between the ultimate application, call it agentic application if you want, down through the software stack and into the hardware'.

CUSTOMERS NOW PUSH ON ACCESS SPEED PER DRIVE, NOT ONLY CAPACITY - AND ON DATA SOVEREIGNTY. Asked what could shift the conversation three years out, Chairman Dave Mosley put two vectors on the roadmap: 'We're going to keep driving density, and we think we can, which is great, makes the data centers more efficient. We can also drive the technology that actually makes the data more accessible on each individual hard drive or at the system level. We're going to get pushed very hard on that because it's not only more data, it's also data faster, which are the vectors that our customers are really driving.' Beyond the drive itself he flagged data protection and locality - 'making sure that you have the right data in the right location, that it's actually my data and not shared with everybody in the world... Sometimes it's called sovereign data' - as a topic he expects to get much more discussion. Closing: 'These trends are happening in our favor, and we know there is a lot riding on our shoulders. We have to keep our technology going forward so that we can keep gaining efficiency.'
